grounding.states: NIH: short-term melatonin use appears safe for most people; long-term safety information is lacking
grounding.from: The NIH says short-term melatonin use appears safe for most people, but information on long-term safety is lacking.

grounding.states: UC Davis: short-term means one to two months
grounding.from: UC Davis defines short-term as one to two months.

grounding.states: GoodRx: avoid taking it daily for more than a week or two at a time
grounding.from: GoodRx advises against taking it daily for more than a week or two at a time.

grounding.states: Adult dose figures conflict: 3 to 5 mg (GoodRx) versus 0.3 to 1 mg (Yale New Haven Health doctor)
grounding.from: GoodRx says the most common adult dose is about 3 to 5 mg, taken 1 to 2 hours before bed. Yale New Haven Health quotes a doctor saying adults should take only 0.3 to 1 mg, and not long-term.

grounding.states: AHA abstract, Nov 2025, preliminary: 130,828 adults, heart failure in 4.6% of long-term users vs 2.7% of non-users over five years; observational, cannot prove cause; not peer-reviewed
grounding.from: It reviewed records of 130,828 adults and found heart failure in 4.6% of long-term melatonin users versus 2.7% of non-users over five years. The AHA says the study cannot prove cause and effect. The AHA also says the findings are preliminary because abstracts at its meetings are not peer-reviewed.

grounding.states: Some experts think the heart link may reflect poor sleep rather than melatonin
grounding.from: Scientific American reports that some experts think the results may reflect the effects of poor sleep rather than melatonin.

grounding.states: Caution for older adults and people with previous low-impact fractures (fracture risk)
grounding.from: The PMC review says the possible fracture risk is a reason to use melatonin with caution in older adults and in people with previous low-impact fractures.

grounding.states: Side effects and drug interactions; check with a doctor or pharmacist before starting
grounding.from: GoodRx says melatonin has side effects and drug interactions. It suggests checking with a healthcare team before starting.

grounding.states: Long-term sleep problems can point to an underlying condition that may worsen without medical input
grounding.from: GoodRx also says long-term sleep problems often point to an underlying condition, and that taking melatonin long term without medical input could let that condition worsen.

value.answer: For most adults, short-term use looks fine. The NIH says it appears safe for most people, but long-term safety data is thin. UC Davis calls short-term one to two months, and GoodRx says not every night for more than a week or two, so the sources don't quite agree on the limit. There's also a new heart concern, but it's preliminary: an American Heart Association abstract from November 2025 linked a year or more of use in people with chronic insomnia to more heart failure. It's observational, so it can't show cause, it hasn't been peer-reviewed, and some experts think poor sleep may explain it. Dosing advice conflicts too, from 0.3 to 1 mg up to 3 to 5 mg, so check the right dose with a doctor or pharmacist, especially if you take other medication, are older, or have ongoing sleep trouble, since that can point to something underlying.
